### C.2 Comparison to previous results

The defect superconformal index for a different type of surface defect preserving the same symmetry (B.1) was studied in [96] for ${\rm U}(N)$ SYM. Here the surface defect is described directly by coupling 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ hypermultiplets in the fundamental representation of ${\rm U}(N)$ to the bulk 4d ${\rm U}(N)$ SYM, we will refer to it as the free-hyper surface defect. This is physically distinct from the Gukov-Witten surface defects we study in this paper which have well-defined holographic duals as D3-branes in the type IIB string theory. Nonetheless, at the level of the 4d-2d description of the surface defect, the free-hyper surface defect only differs from the GW surface defect of the Levi-type $L=[1,N-1]$ by the 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ $\rm{U}(1)$ gauge interaction on the defect worldvolume. Therefore we naively expect to obtain the same answer in the leading large $N$ limit. Below we connect the computation in [96] to our calculation here and comment on the differences and relations.

In [96], a different set of linearly independent bosonic charges was chosen to express the defect superconformal index (1.23),

$$ \mathcal{I}_{{\mathcal{D}}}=\textrm{Tr}_{\mathcal{H}_{{\mathcal{D}}}(S^{3})}\left[(-1)^{F}e^{-\beta\{{\mathcal{Q}},{\mathcal{Q}}^{\dagger}\}}t^{2(\tilde{E}+\tilde{j}_{1})}y^{2\tilde{j}_{2}}v^{\tilde{R}_{2}}w^{\tilde{R}_{3}}\right]\,. $$

These charges in [96] (which we denote with an extra tilde) are related to the ones here by,

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}=E\,,\quad\tilde{j}_{1}=\frac{J_{1}+J_{2}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{j}_{2}=\frac{J_{1}-J_{2}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{R}_{1}=\frac{R_{2}+R_{1}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{R}_{2}=\frac{R_{1}-R_{2}}{2}\,, \displaystyle\tilde{R}_{3}=\frac{R_{2}-R_{3}}{2}\,,\quad\tilde{C}=-J_{2}-\frac{R_{1}}{2}\,. $$

The relation between the chemical potentials in [96] and our convention follows by comparing (1.23) and (C.3),

$$ e^{2\pi i\sigma}=t^{3}y\,,\quad e^{2\pi i\tau}=\frac{t^{3}}{y}\,,\quad e^{2\pi i\Delta_{1}}=t^{2}v\,,\quad e^{2\pi i\Delta_{2}}=\frac{t^{2}w}{v}\,. $$

By explicitly enumerating the single-particle letters, the contribution to the defect index from the hypermultiplets $(B,\tilde{B})$ is obtained in the form of a Plethystic exponential, which then produces an explicit form of the modified unitary matrix model for the defect index [96].

Let us point out a few differences between the 2d index ${\mathcal{I}}_{\text{2d}}$ expression (3.14) considered in this paper for the GW surface defect and the Plethystic exponential expression for the free-hyper defect insertion in [96]. Firstly, the bosonic zero-modes of the hypermultiplet fields $b,\tilde{b}$ were manually excluded from the 2d index calculation in [96], while these fields have been taken into account in (3.14). At a technical level, including these contributions makes it possible to write the Plethystic exponential in terms of the $\theta_{0}$ -functions that produce the desired modular and elliptic properties (in particular periodicity upon certain integer shifts of the chemical potentials, see e.g. (F.1)). Furthermore we find that including these modes is crucial to reproduce the gravity answer in the holographic dual.3838 38 As mentioned in the Introduction, the GW surface defect is dual to the probe D3 brane with Neumann boundary condition for its AdS3 gauge field. On the other hand, we expect the analog of the free-hyper surface defect in the SU $(N)$ SYM to be dual to the case with Dirichlet boundary condition for the AdS3 gauge field. In particular, there is a residual U $(1)$ global symmetry and decoupled 2d degrees of freedom on this free-hyper defect, unlike the GW surface defect. We thank Ofer Aharony for discussions on this point. Secondly, the contribution from the 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ vector multiplet $(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{S})$ is missing for the free-hyper defect in [96] by construction. Relatedly, unlike the GW surface defect, the ${\rm U}(1)$ subgroup of the ${\rm U}(N)$ symmetry of the free hypermultiplets is gauged not by the 2d vector multiplet but instead by the 4d vector multiplet in the bulk SYM [96], and consequently the corresponding 2d contribution ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm 2d}$ to the defect index (compared to (3.14)) has not been projected to the ${\rm U}(1)$ -singlet sector.

### C.3 2d contribution to the defect index from the elliptic genus

Here we briefly review the calculation of the elliptic genus of 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ SQED with a pair of hypermultiplets $(B,\tilde{B})$ with charge $\pm 1$ . Upon spectral flow, this will produce the 2d contribution ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm 2d}$ to the defect index for the Gukov-Witten surface defect that corresponds to a probe D3-brane in the bulk.

The elliptic genus is an important invariant defined for general 2d ${\mathcal{N}}=(0,1)$ supersymmetric QFTs (SQFTs) that is preserved under supersymmetry preserving deformations such as supersymmetric RG flows. It is typically defined in the RR sector of the 2d SQFT where the left- and right-moving fermions have periodic boundary conditions along the spatial ${\rm S}^{1}$ . Here, for the ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ GLSM that describes the surface defect, the fully refined elliptic genus takes the following form,

$$ \mathcal{I}_{\text{RR}}\equiv\text{Tr}_{\text{RR}}\,(-1)^{F}e^{2\pi i\tau_{\text{2d}}L_{0}}e^{-2\pi i\bar{\tau}_{\text{2d}}\bar{L}_{0}}e^{2\pi iz_{\text{R}}J_{0}}e^{2\pi i\chi J_{A}}e^{2\pi iuC}\,, $$

where the bosonic charges and chemical potentials are as defined in Appendix C.1.

General discussions on how to compute the elliptic genus for GLSMs can be found in [88, 125, 124]. The main point is that ${\mathcal{I}}_{\rm RR}$ can be written as an integral over the holonomies of the gauge fields on the spacetime torus $T^{2}$ with complex structure $\tau_{\rm 2d}=\sigma$ where the integrand is given by a product of one-loop determinants that capture the fluctuations. This general formula was derived in [125, 124] by supersymmetric localization (see also the review [173]). Here, specializing to the case of ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ SQED with $N$ unit-charge hypermultiplets, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{\text{RR}}= \displaystyle\int d{\bm{u}}\,\frac{2\pi(\eta(\tau_{\text{2d}}))^{3}}{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-z_{\text{R}})}\frac{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-2\chi)}{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|z_{\text{R}}-2\chi)} \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-{\bm{u}}+u_{i}+\chi-z_{\text{R}}\right)\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|{\bm{u}}-u_{i}+\chi-z_{\text{R}}\right)}{\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|-{\bm{u}}+u_{i}+\chi\right)\theta_{1}\left(\tau_{\text{2d}}|{\bm{u}}-u_{i}+\chi\right)}\,, $$

where $\eta(\tau_{\text{2d}})$ denotes the Dedekind eta function and $\theta_{1}(\tau_{\rm 2d}|z)$ is a Jacobi theta function. The two terms on the first line of (C.7) come from $S$ and $\mathcal{V}$ respectively in the abelian ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ vector multiplet. The terms in the second line account for the contribution from the hypermuliplets $(B,\tilde{B})$ . The integral is over the complex variable ${\bm{u}}$ which encodes the independent holonomies of the abelian gauge field on $T^{2}$ ,

$$ {\bm{u}}=\oint_{S^{1}}dx^{0}\,A_{0}-\sigma\oint_{S^{1}}dx^{1}\,A_{1}\,,\quad{\bm{u}}\in{{\mathbb{C}}/({\mathbb{Z}}+\sigma{\mathbb{Z}})}\,, $$

where the periodic identifications on $\bm{u}$ come from the large gauge transformations.

The complex holonomy integral (e.g. (C.7)) can be further reduced to a contour integral on the torus of abelian holonomies and the latter can be evaluated by the Jeffery-Kirwan residue prescription [124, 125, 173]. In the case of ${\mathcal{N}}=(4,4)$ SQED, this amounts to collecting the residues at the $N$ simple poles in (C.7) associated to the positive-charged field at ${\bm{u}}=u_{i}-\chi$ . The final answer is

$$ \mathcal{I}_{\text{RR}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{i\neq j}\frac{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij}+z_{\text{R}}-2\chi)\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij}-z_{\text{R}})}{\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij})\theta_{1}(\tau_{\text{2d}}|u_{ij}-2\chi)}\,, $$

where $u_{ij}\equiv u_{i}-u_{j}$ . This expression already appeared in [125] and is here written in terms of the chemical potentials in our conventions.

Instead of doing the integral over holonomy $\bm{u}$ exactly using the Jeffery-Kirwan residue prescription, we can also fix the value of $\bm{u}$ , perform the large $N$ analysis of the integrand in (C.7) and eventually integrate over $\bm{u}$ . We found that both in the empty AdS phase and the black hole phase, $\bm{u}=0$ dominates the integral. This justifies our choice in the gravity analysis of Section 2 to focus on the simplest D3-brane configuration with no worldvolume gauge field turned on.

## Appendix E Field theory analysis in the $\sigma=\tau$ limit

In the main part of this paper, we focused on the range of chemical potentials (3.17), where the 2d index formula (3.16) has a convergent Plethystic exponential expression, assuming that the ${\rm SU}(N)$ holonomies take real values. Within this range, we find agreement between the bulk and boundary analysis.

However, the range of chemical potential (3.17) excludes the special limit $\sigma=\tau,\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}=\Delta_{3}=(2\sigma-1)/3$ . If we naively apply the index formula (3.16) outside the range (3.17) and in particular to the $\sigma=\tau$ limit, we encounter subtleties that we are not sure how to resolve. Intriguingly, instead of the more intricate analysis for the black hole saddle, it is for the thermal AdS saddle that we appear to find an surprising answer. In this appendix we present the puzzling computation and discuss some possible interpretations. We leave a satisfying resolution to future study.

For convenience, here we write down the expression for the 2d index that we will evaluate (after specifying to the case $\sigma=\tau$ ):

$$ \mathcal{I}_{2d}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ji}+\frac{\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ij}+\frac{2\sigma}{3}+\frac{2}{3})}{\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ji}-\frac{\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{3})\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ij})}. $$

### E.1 Thermal AdS saddle

As explained in section 3, the thermal AdS saddle corresponds to the eigenvalue distribution $u_{j}=\frac{j}{N},j=0,...,N-1$ . For the purpose of evaluating the large $N$ limit of $\mathcal{I}_{2d}$ , we’d like to write the $\theta_{0}$ functions into Plethystic exponential form. Since all $u_{i}$ are real, in order to make $\theta_{0}$ -functions have convergent Plethystic exponentials, we need to shift the argument of $\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ji}-\frac{\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{3})$ using identity (G.5)

$$ \theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|u_{ji}-\frac{\sigma}{3}\right.-\frac{1}{3}\right)=-e^{2\pi i\left(u_{ji}-\frac{1}{3}\sigma-\frac{1}{3}\right)}\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|u_{ji}+\frac{2\sigma}{3}\right.-\frac{1}{3}\right). $$

After this shift on the argument, all $\theta_{0}$ -functions appear in (E.1) have valid Plethystic exponentials. Based on the same argument made in section 3.2, Plethystic exponentials evaluated at the thermal AdS saddle always contribute $e^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ factors to the 2d index. Therefore, the large- $N$ contributions purely come from the prefactor in (E.2). In this case, we find that

$$ -\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle=-2\pi iN\left(\frac{1}{3}\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right)+\mathcal{O}(1), $$

which has a nonvanishing $O(N)$ term. It seems to suggest a nonzero brane action, despite being on the thermal AdS background. We are not aware of a possible interpretation of this nonzero action.

One possible resolution to this is that one should first evaluate the large $N$ limit of the field theory expression within the range (3.17), then analytically continue the large $N$ action to the $\sigma=\tau$ limit. This would lead to an answer that is simply zero which agrees with what we would expect from gravity. However, it is unclear to us what the physical motivation of such a prescription is. Of course, another possibility is that (E.3) does have a gravity interpretation.

### E.2 Black hole saddle

When $\sigma=\tau$ , the supersymmetric black hole solution is associated to the $(1,0)$ saddle of the matrix integral[33], which can also be derived from the roots of the Bethe-ansatz equation[58, 25]. The eigenvalue $u_{j}$ is distributed uniformly on the line in $\sigma$ direction, i.e. $u_{j}=\frac{j}{N}\sigma,j=0,...,N-1$ . This distribution of $u_{j}$ is different from directly the distribution obtained by taking the collinear limit $\sigma\rightarrow\tau$ of the parallelogram ansatz used in Section 3. In [48], the relation between the solutions of two ansatz was studied, and it was shown that the large- $N$ contribution from both approaches agree. In this part of discussion, we use the saddle-point distribution from BAEs for simplicity, and in the end we will see that the result is consistent with the collinear limit of the analytic continuation of the result in Section 3. Note that the expression (E.1) is invariant under $u_{i}\rightarrow u_{i}+\sigma$ shift, all terms in the summation over $i$ should be identical. In the large- $N$ limit, we rewrite the 2d index into the following integral expression

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}dx\left[-\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|x\sigma+\frac{\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right.\right)-\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|-x\sigma+\frac{2\sigma}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\right.\right)\right. \displaystyle\left.+\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|x\sigma-\frac{\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\right.\right)+\log\theta_{0}\left(\sigma\left|-x\sigma\right.\right)\right]. $$

In order to evaluate this integral, we could adopt the same procedure as we use in Appendix D to write the $\theta_{0}$ -functions into convergent Plethystic exponentials by shifting the arguments suitably. After performing the shifts, we decompose the integral into the following parts

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}= \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{1}dx\log\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma+\frac{2}{3}\right)}{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma-\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma\right)} \displaystyle+2\pi i\int_{\frac{2}{3}}^{1}dx\,\left(x\sigma-\frac{2\sigma}{3}-\frac{1}{6}\right)-2\pi i\int_{\frac{2}{3}}^{1}dx\,\left(-x\sigma+\frac{2\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{6}\right) \displaystyle+2\pi i\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{3}}dx\,\left(x\sigma-\frac{\sigma}{3}+\frac{1}{6}\right)+2\pi i\int_{0}^{1}dx\,\left(-x\sigma+\frac{1}{2}\right). $$

The first line admits the convergent Plethystic exponential expression, so we can integrate out $x$ and write the result in terms of dilogarithm functions

$$ \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{1}dx\log\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma+\frac{2}{3}\right)}{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|x\sigma-\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|(1-x)\sigma\right)}= \displaystyle\frac{i}{2\pi\sigma}\left[\text{Li}_{2}(e^{\frac{4\pi i}{3}})+\text{Li}_{2}(e^{-\frac{4\pi i}{3}})-2\text{Li}_{2}(1)\right], $$

where we use the series expansion of dilogarithm $\text{Li}_{2}(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{z^{n}}{n^{2}}$ . For dilogarithm function, we have the following useful identity

$$ \textrm{Li}_{2}(e^{2\pi iz})+\textrm{Li}_{2}(e^{-2\pi iz})=2\pi^{2}B_{2}(z),\quad 0\leq\textrm{Re}(z)<1, $$

where $B_{2}(z)$ is the second Bernoulli polynomial. By applying this identity to the dilogarithms in the $-\log\mathcal{I}_{\text{2d}}$ expression, we obtain the following leading term in the large- $N$ expansion

$$ -\frac{\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle}{N}=-\frac{2\pi i}{9\sigma}-\frac{8\pi i}{9}(\sigma-1)=-\frac{2\pi i(2\sigma-1)^{2}}{9\sigma}, $$

which agrees with the result derived in (3.43) provided that $\sigma$ is equal to $\tau$ . Therefore, in this case, the final expression (E.8) is still consistent with the D3-brane effective action (2.37) evaluated in the black hole background.

## Appendix F Defects on shifted chemical potential saddle points

As we have mentioned in the main text, an important conceptual point in the recent discussion of the ${1\over 16}$ -BPS index and its gravity dual is the importance of saddle points with shifted chemical potentials. These are gravity solutions with the same fugacities but different chemical potentials at infinity, and the sum over them is important in reproducing the expected periodicity of the field theory index. This is very clear if we wrote the field theory expression in terms of a trace. After transforming to a microcanonical ensemble in the charges, this periodicity property implies the correct discreteness of the charge spectrum (in the original superconformal index or in the case with a surface operator insertion). The existence of these extra saddles is thus a field theory motivated constraint on the “sum over geometries” as expected of a gravitational path integral. In cases such as the near extremal or near BPS limits of the gravity path integral, the sum over these shifted saddles is not suppressed, and they have important consequences for the low energy physics [74, 49, 127, 75].

Given the chemical potentials $\sigma,\tau,\Delta_{a},a=1,2,3$ on the field theory side, one can generally consider infinitely many gravity solutions with chemical potentials $\sigma_{g},\,\tau_{g},\,\Delta_{a,g},\,a=1,2,3$ shifted relative to the field theory ones by independent integers (while satisfying the constraint $\sigma_{g}+\tau_{g}-\Delta_{1,g}-\Delta_{2,g}-\Delta_{3,g}=\pm 1$ ). Here we used subscript $g$ to highlight that the chemical potentials showing up in gravity can be distinct from the ones at the boundary. Even though these gravity solutions formally exist, their stability and the convergence of the sum over them are generally unclear. More essential to our consideration here, the full characterization of these solutions on the field theory side, in particular, in the language of large $N$ saddle points for the unitary matrix integral [48] (see e.g. [45] for a different approach using Thermal Bethe Ansatz), is still under active research and have not been fully understood to our best knowledge.

It is natural to wonder about how the defect/D3-brane behaves on these other saddles. We will restrict our attention to the case where

$$ \sigma_{g}=\sigma+3n_{1},\quad\tau_{g}=\tau+3n_{2},\quad\Delta_{1,g}=\Delta_{2,g}=\Delta_{3,g}=\frac{\sigma+\tau-1}{3}+n_{1}+n_{2},\quad n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}, $$

so that the black hole solution still has the same R-charges and can be described by the same metric as in Section 2.4040 40 Notice that not all of these gravity solutions are stable. For the case with $\sigma=\tau$ , it was shown in [45] that the action can be lower by adding wrapped Euclidean D3 branes unless $\sigma_{g}=\tau_{g}$ . We thank Ofer Aharony and Ohad Mamroud for comments on this point. The only difference is that the chemical potentials in Section 2 are now replaced by the ones with subscript $g$ and the rest of the analysis goes through. Therefore, following (2.37), the action of the D3-brane on the shifted gravity saddles, after regularization, is

$$ I_{D3,\textrm{E, finite}}=-2\pi iN\frac{(\sigma_{g}+\tau_{g}-1)^{2}}{9\sigma_{g}}=-2\pi iN\frac{(\sigma+\tau+3(n_{1}+n_{2})-1)^{2}}{9(\sigma+3n_{1})}. $$

On the field theory side, [48] proposed a family of large $N$ saddle points that naturally correspond to (F.1). These saddle points are characterized by a uniform parallelogram distribution of holonomies $u_{i}$ , similar to what we considered in (3.3), but with two edges of the parallelogram given by $\sigma+3n_{1},\tau+3n_{2}$ . It was claimed in [48] that this new parallelogram saddle would satisfy the large $N$ saddle point equations of the unitary matrix model, with the shifted chemical potentials, namely $\sigma+3n_{1},\tau+3n_{2},\Delta_{a}+n_{1}+n_{2},a=1,2,3$ satisfying the same inequalities that the chemical potentials should satisfy for the original saddle point.4141 41 See (2.41) of [48] for the detailed form of the inequalitites. We thank Seok Kim for correspondence on these points. Therefore, we have

$$ \langle\mathcal{D}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ji}+\frac{2(\sigma+3n_{1})}{3}-\frac{\tau+3n_{2}}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ij}+\frac{\sigma+3n_{1}}{3}+\frac{\tau+3n_{2}}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\right)}{\theta_{0}\left(\sigma|u_{ji}+\frac{\sigma+3n_{1}}{3}-\frac{2(\tau+3n_{2})}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\right)\theta_{0}(\sigma|u_{ij})}, $$

where $u_{i}=u_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}=\frac{\hat{i}}{\sqrt{N}}(\sigma+3n_{1})+\frac{\hat{j}}{\sqrt{N}}(\tau+3n_{2})$ . One might be puzzled by the explicit shift of the chemical potentials in (F.3), but since we have $\theta_{0}(\sigma|x+1)=\theta_{0}(\sigma|x)$ , the shifts in (F.3) should not affect the final answer, given that $n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}$ . This is of course true, but the benefit of (F.3) is to highlight that the shifted chemical potentials $\sigma+3n_{1},...$ should be within the same range as the chemical potentials for which the discussion in Section 3.3 would be valid. The calculation then follows exactly the discussion in Section 3.3, with the chemical potentials replaced by the shifted ones. From (3.43), this yields a final answer

$$ -\log\,\langle\mathcal{D}\rangle=-2\pi iN\frac{(\sigma+\tau+3(n_{1}+n_{2})-1)^{2}}{9(\sigma+3n_{1})}, $$

which agrees with (F.2).

However, we want to highlight an unsatisfying feature of this discussion. Generally, after we fix the values of $\sigma,\tau,\Delta_{a}$ which lie within the inequalities in [48], the shifted chemical potentials $\sigma+3n_{1},\tau+3n_{2},\Delta_{a}+n_{1}+n_{2}$ will not satisfy the same inequalities and therefore we cannot apply the parallelogram ansatz. To make it more clear, in the above field theory calculation, we are not considering the shifted saddles for the same chemical potentials, but rather shifted saddles for correspondingly different chemical potentials. This appears to be different from the gravity picture where we can consider both the original saddle and the shifted ones for a fixed set of chemical potential. Therefore, the results in this appendix shouldn’t be taken as a match between field theory side and the gravity side, but rather as only preliminary evidence. Nonetheless, we would like to emphasize that the difficulty of relating the two is already present at the level of the original BPS index, and not particularly related to the added defect. It would also be useful to understand whether one can apply different techniques, such as the Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz [45] to compute the 4d-2d index.

## Appendix G Conventions and relations for $\theta$ -functions

The Plethystic exponential, which usually appears in the index calculation, is defined as follows:

$$ \textrm{PE}\left(\frac{a}{1-q}\right)\equiv\exp\left[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}\frac{a^{n}}{1-q^{n}}\right]. $$

Provided the above definition, we can associate the Plethystic exponential to the $q$ -Pochhammer symbol

$$ (a;q)_{\infty}\equiv\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-aq^{k})=\frac{1}{\textrm{PE}\left(\frac{a}{1-q}\right)} $$

We introduce one useful special function $\theta_{0}$ in terms of the product of two $q$ -Pochhammer symbols

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)=\left(e^{2\pi iu};e^{2\pi i\tau}\right)_{\infty}\left(e^{2\pi i(\tau-u)};e^{2\pi i\tau}\right)_{\infty} $$

By massaging the two Plethystic exponentials in (G.3) together, we obtain a series expansion for $\log{\theta_{0}}$

$$ \log\theta_{0}(\tau|u)=-i\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\cos{n\pi(2u-\tau)}}{n\sin{n\pi\tau}}. $$

Note that the above Plethystic exponential expression does not always have a convergent exponent. The formula (G.1) is only valid when $|q|,|a|<1$ . Therefore, the $\theta_{0}$ -function can be rewritten as a Plethystic exponential only if $\text{Im}(\tau)>0,\,0<\text{Im}(u)<\text{Im}(\tau)$ . The same criterion also works for the series expansion of $\log{\theta_{0}}$ .

The $\theta_{0}$ -function has the following quasi-periodicity property:

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)=\theta_{0}(\tau|u+1)=-e^{2\pi iu}\theta_{0}(\tau|u+\tau). $$

Moreover, the $\theta_{0}$ -function possesses a few modular properties under the transformations $\tau\rightarrow\tau+1$ ( $T$ ) and $u\rightarrow\frac{u}{\tau},\,\tau\rightarrow-\frac{1}{\tau}$ ( $S$ )

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{0}(\tau|u)= \displaystyle\theta_{0}(\tau+1|u), \displaystyle\theta_{0}(\tau|u)= \displaystyle e^{\pi iB_{2,2}(u|\tau,-1)}\theta_{0}\left(-\frac{1}{\tau}\left|\frac{u}{\tau}\right.\right), $$

where $B_{2,2}(u|\tau,-1)$ is the multiple Bernoulli polynomial defined as follows:

$$ B_{2,2}(u|\tau,-1)=-\frac{B_{2}(u+1)}{\tau}+B_{1}(u+1)-\frac{\tau}{6}. $$

The $B_{1}(x)=x-\frac{1}{2}$ and $B_{2}(x)=x^{2}-x+\frac{1}{6}$ are ordinary Bernoulli polynomials.

Besides the $\theta_{0}$ -function, we introduce the ordinary Jacobi Theta function $\theta_{1}$ , which can be obtained from the $\theta_{0}$ -function via the following identity:

$$ \theta_{1}(\tau|u)=ie^{-i\pi(u-\tau/4)}(q;q)\theta_{0}(\tau|u). $$

The Jacobi theta function $\theta_{1}$ has the following double quasi-periodicity:

$$ \theta_{1}(\tau|u+a+b\tau)=(-1)^{a+b}e^{-2\pi ibu-i\pi b^{2}\tau}\theta_{1}(\tau|u). $$

Here we summarize the zeroes and poles of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ , which is useful in performing the contour integral over the worldvolume gauge field. $\theta_{0}(\sigma|u)$ has no poles, while it has zeroes at $u=a+b\tau$ . The derivative of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ near $u=0$ is

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)^{\prime}|_{u=0}=-2\pi i(q;q)^{2}. $$

According to the residue theorem, we have the following contour integral

$$ \oint_{u=0}\frac{du}{\theta_{0}(\tau|u)}=-\frac{1}{(q;q)^{2}}. $$

Another important identity of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ is

$$ \theta_{0}(\tau|u)=-e^{2\pi iu}\theta_{0}(\tau|-u). $$

This property can be derived directly from the definition of $\theta_{0}(\tau|u)$ in (G.3).
